newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish president to block lower house tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Polish president to block lower house tax cut.

text.p: Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski will use all means at his disposal, which include the veto, to block a sharp tax cut for the low paid which could boost inflation and the budget gap, his spokesman said.

Antoni Styrczula said on Tuesday that Kwasniewski hoped the Senate would reverse last week's surprise vote by the lower house to introduce a new 17 percent tax band for the lowest paid, which the finance ministry said would bring a higher deficit and inflation.
Styrczula told a weekly news conference the president supported the government's proposal to lower personal income taxes to 20, 31 and 43 percent in 1997 from the current 21, 33 and 45 percent.
"The president hopes the Senate will correct the decision of the Sejm (lower house)," Styrczula said. "He considers...the best solution is...the scale at 20, 31 and 43 percent."
"The president will use all means available to him to prevent...growth of inflation and the budget deficit," he said.
Pressed to specify whether this might involve vetoing the tax bill, Styrczula said this option was available, but Kwasniewski hoped the Senate would resolve the matter.

Last week, in a move which ambushed the government, the lower house passed the new tax levels with the votes of the opposition and the Polish Peasant Party (PSL) -- smaller partner in the ruling coalition with the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD)
The appalled finance ministry said this tax change would cost the budget 4.6 billion zlotys in lost revenues.
It said the change was impossible to implement without raising the budget deficit, which the government wants to keep flat at 2.8 percent of the gross domestic product next year.

The Peasants later suggested they might reverse their stance in the Senate if they were convinced the plan to slash taxes for the low paid could not be accommodated by the nearly-complete 1997 budget.
The coalition is to meet next week to reach an agreement on next year's taxes before they are voted on by the Senate.
